speaker_role: former admissions officer (led admissions at Swarthmore College; long-time admissions officer at Vanderbilt University)
commercial_incentive: Yes - promotes a paid 'Common App Bootcamp' and a free downloadable brag sheet as lead magnets
key_insights: Counselor letters mainly provide school context, curriculum/rigor explanation, and comparison to peers; students at large public schools with high caseloads are not penalized for shorter/templated counselor letters

Teacher letters carry more student control and should come from teachers who know the student well (not necessarily the one who gave the easiest A) - a hard-won A- or B+ can produce a stronger letter than an easy A
Recommends choosing teachers from core academic subjects taught recently (10th/11th grade), and balancing STEM/humanities letters even for single-discipline applicants like engineers
Advises phrasing recommendation requests as 'Would you feel comfortable writing me a strong letter?' to give teachers an easy way to decline rather than give a lukewarm letter

Suggests preparing a 'brag sheet' for recommenders covering intended major, favorite assignments, growth moments, and challenges - explicitly not honors/awards/activities, and never phrased as instructions for what to write
States some colleges (e.g., Swarthmore, per speaker's own experience) require letters from specific core-subject teachers and will request replacements for non-core-subject letters
Notes recommendation letters are rarely the sole reason for an admit/deny decision but influence how confidently a committee feels about admitting a student
International students without a formal 'counselor' role can have another school official (headmaster, subject teacher, academic advisor) submit materials instead
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker states he has read more than 100,000 recommendation letters over his career
Speaker recommends one additional optional letter beyond the requirement at most, calling more than that repetitive and potentially diluting
notable_or_distinctive: Gives a specific, actionable request script ('Would you feel comfortable writing me a strong letter of recommendation?') designed to let teachers decline gracefully rather than produce a weak letter, plus a detailed breakdown of what a brag sheet should and should not contain.
reliability_notes: Speaker has genuine institutional admissions credentials (named schools, named role), which supports reliability, but the video also functions as a funnel toward his paid bootcamp and downloadable resources, so some framing favors that offer.
